Photograph: Geography Photos/Universal Images Group/Getty Images Oil ‘Astronomical’ fuel price surge hits farmers in UK and US Intensification of Middle East conflict and ongoing Russian export ban sees diesel prices rise 10% in less than a week Joanna Partridge and Alex Daniel Fri 4 Sep 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 05.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Farmers are facing an “astronomical” jump in the price of fuel needed to operate their vehicles and machinery after a surge in diesel costs in the UK and US. Renewed fighting between the US and Iran has driven up the price of crude oil, while last week Russia extended a ban on diesel exports, further pushing up market prices. An intensification of Middle East hostilities over the weekend pushed fuel costs even higher for farmers, said Alex Harrison, a fuel buyer at Fram Farmers, a not-for-profit farmer-owned co-operative. The price of all fuels had gone up by “an astronomical amount in just a few days”, she said, rising by between 10p and 14p a litre since Monday. This represents about a 10% increase in the cost of red diesel – fuel used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate to standard diesel – which currently costs about £1.10 a litre. The average price of diesel for UK motorists had climbed to 183.5p a litre on Thursday, according to government data , up from 164.5p in mid-July. The volatility in oil wholesale markets has left farmers struggling to decide how much fuel to buy and when, with many calling for advice from Fram Farmers, which represents more than 1,400 farm businesses across the UK. While the harvest peak demand for red diesel and other fuels has passed, many growers traditionally buy more fuel at this time of year as they begin to prepare their land for winter. “This latest spike has really caught everybody by surprise and hit them quite hard because it’s been such a large spike and because of the time of year,” Harrison said. Farmers are “trying to decide what’s best to do, how to order for [managing their] cashflow”. The co-operative’s members have changed their buying patterns since the outbreak of war in Iran sent oil prices soaring. Harrison said: “A lot of people have ordered in much smaller increments and more often, as they are trying to hedge their bets a little.” View image in fullscreen Co-operative members had been ordering fuel ‘in much smaller increments and more often’, said Alex Harrison of Fram Farmers. Photograph: Henry Arden/Getty Images/Image Source The rise in diesel prices comes amid a squeeze on global refining capacity. Russia, which normally supplies about 10% of the world’s diesel despite western sanctions, has been hit by Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries in August, prompting the export ban extension. That has been compounded by a wider increase in the price of crude oil. The international benchmark Brent crude was trading at close to $97 a barrel on Thursday, its highest point in about six weeks. There was a major flare-up in attacks in the Middle East last weekend, the first US strikes since July. Two Saudi supertankers were hit in the strait of Hormuz late on Monday, fuelling concerns of a longer-term return to hostilities. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Tehran warned ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the Iranian strikes. US diesel prices have climbed to their highest level in about four years. The average price reached $5.78 a gallon on Thursday, according to the AAA motoring organisation, up 54% since the war began. Diesel last traded close to this level in 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Small businesses and larger companies that rely on vehicle fleets, such as delivery firms and construction companies, will also face higher running costs as a result. Back in the UK, the price of paraffin, or heating oil – widely used on farms to heat buildings including farmhouses and barns – is also higher, at a time of year when many households, mostly in rural communities that are not connected to the gas network, would usually be starting to think about filling their tanks ahead of the winter. The current price for paraffin is close to £1 a litre, compared with prices of about 60p a litre just before the Iran war. https://aa.com.tr/en/turkiye/turkish-f-1.text: Türkiye Turkish F-16 jets land at Latvian military base as part of NATO mission - 2 Turkish fighter jets flew to Latvia from Amari Air Base in Estonia as part of NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission Seyit Şamil Kurt 21 August 2026 • Update : 21 August 2026 İSTANBUL Two Turkish F-16 fighter jets landed at Latvia's Lielvarde Military Base on Friday as part of NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission, according to the Latvian Defense Ministry. The aircraft flew to Latvia from Amari Air Base in neighboring Estonia, where a Turkish contingent is supporting NATO's mission to safeguard the airspace of the Baltic states, the ministry said in a statement. Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis, Türkiye's Ambassador to Latvia Ahmet Cemil Miroglu, and senior Latvian military officials attended an event marking the aircraft’s arrival. Melnis said the presence of Turkish fighter jets in Latvia demonstrates NATO's readiness to protect allied airspace and respond to potential threats. "The presence of Allied forces strengthens the security of Latvia and NATO's entire eastern flank, while sending a clear message of the Alliance's unity and the strength of our collective defence," he said. The ministry said Italy assumed responsibility for the latest rotation of NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission at Siauliai Air Base in Lithuania on July 31, taking over from French and Romanian contingents. The Italian-led rotation is being supported by the Turkish contingent operating from Amari Air Base in Estonia. The three Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, all of them former Soviet republics, have a combined population of a little over 6 million people. https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: BERLIN — Germany’s far right is moving to turn its landslide election victory into a knockout blow against Friedrich Merz and his beleaguered conservatives — and the chancellor appears at a loss over how to respond. Merz seemed to have no clear plan for saving himself and his party as his government confronted its biggest political crisis yet, beyond ambiguous promises to become a better, more empathetic politician 16 months into his chancellorship. “We are all deeply shocked,” Merz said Monday, after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) reached a new high in Saxony-Anhalt’s weekend election while support for his Christian Democratic Union fell by more than half . “This is the worst election defeat the CDU has suffered in years — or even decades,” the chancellor added. “Of course, there will have to be consequences.” Advertisement Advertisement But what those consequences will be remains uncertain. Merz’s dismal approval ratings and the AfD’s convincing win have fueled speculation that his conservatives could seek a Kanzlertausch , or “chancellor swap,” to revive their political fortunes. But Merz said Monday that he would remain in office and stay the course on economic reforms he argues are long overdue and will, with time, solve the country’s economic problems. The AfD has made little secret of its intent to turn the election loss into a still greater debacle for Merz. The far-right party is openly courting conservative lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt to defect and join its ranks — a strategy aimed not only at securing the three additional seats it needs to govern alone, but also at fracturing the conservatives and breaking Merz’s control of his party. “The conservative bloc will never again be able to win a federal election, that is a fact,” AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel said in Berlin on Monday. “The gap between us and them is already at 10 percent, and my stated goal is to significantly widen that gap in the shortest possible time.” Merz on Monday acknowledged that he is part of the problem. Only 9 percent of people voting in Saxony-Anhalt approved of his performance as chancellor, according to one exit poll for German public television. “I know that my persona, too, has been a recurring topic in this election campaign,” Merz said. Germans are anxious about their economic wellbeing and security in turbulent times, he went on, adding: “We must try — myself included — to connect more deeply with people, including their full range of emotions.” Under pressure The pressure on Merz is likely only to build in the next weeks, particularly as elections loom in two eastern regions on Sept. 20. Merz’s CDU is headed for clear defeat in the state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania, where the AfD is ahead of all other parties. In Berlin, where the CDU is currently governing, the party is likely to fall out of power to a coalition of left-wing parties. Advertisement Advertisement With four more state elections set for next year, conservatives face a clear choice: continue confronting the rising far right under a deeply unpopular chancellor, or fundamentally change course with a new leader at the helm. Merz appeared to acknowledge the dilemma his party is facing. “This election result is causing major upheaval, not only in our country, but also within my party,” he said Monday. “I take this extremely seriously, and I intend to do my best over the coming days and weeks to personally address the gravity of the situation.” While most of the talk of replacing Merz is taking place in private, signs of conservative dissatisfaction with Merz’s leadership are beginning to spill out into the open. Alice Weidel speaks to the media in Berlin on Sept. 7, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images “Anyone who wants to regain trust and credibility must, in the wake of such a result, question everything,” CDU lawmaker Sepp Müller wrote in a social media post . “After a result like this, we cannot simply carry on as usual,” Gordon Schnieder, the CDU state premier of Rhineland-Palatinate, wrote on X . “If the democratic center wants to regain trust, we must start with ourselves. It is not up to the people to better understand our politics. We must deliver what people expect from politics: less conflict, clear decisions, and concrete results.” ‘Matter of compassion’ The AfD is attacking the chancellor on multiple policy fronts — hitting him on migration, blaming his energy policies for the country’s industrial malaise and pushing for the restoration of cheap energy flows from Russia. Advertisement Advertisement But many of the AfD’s most effective attacks are merely tactical. Even as the AfD seeks to win power in Saxony-Anhalt by attempting to peel off conservative defectors, the party is presenting itself as willing to work with the CDU, knowing full well that Merz would not sanction a collapse of the “firewall” that keeps centrist parties from cooperating with the far right. This allows the AfD to simultaneously attack Merz as ignoring the will of the people in the face of the party’s surging popularity, while also depicting conservatives as leftists in disguise for preferring to work with an array of left-wing parties. The election in Saxony-Anhalt illustrates the strategic dilemma the CDU faces — and one the AfD is benefiting from. To avoid governing with the AfD, the CDU would theoretically have to work with every other party in state parliament, all of them on the political left, including the far left. As conservatives buckle under the strain of governing alongside ideological opposites, the AfD hopes that growing divisions over the firewall will ultimately bring about Merz’s downfall. “People have lost confidence in the party,” the AfD’s Weidel said Monday. “Before elections, they always promise one thing. And after the elections, they do the exact opposite. And that’s how every party loses the acceptance and trust of its voters. No chancellor before has been as unpopular as Friedrich Merz, who has become a major obstacle to Germany’s prosperous development.” Tino Chrupalla, the AfD’s other national leader, said that if the CDU does not abandon the firewall, it would mark the party’s end. If the party “continue down this path,” he said, “then in the short term there will no longer be a CDU in eastern Germany.” Advertisement Advertisement While these AfD’s attack lines are proving highly effective, Merz offered no clear plan on Monday for countering them — other than, in effect, becoming a better politician. “This isn’t just a matter of rational political understanding — it’s also a matter of compassion, empathy, and emotions,” a somber-sounding Merz told reporters in Berlin. “I’m not the type to wear my emotions on my sleeve every day, but the public wants to see different answers.” He acknowledged he had failed to connect with voters — but suggested there was still time for him to learn. “It’s certainly true that I have this problem — and you can see it in the polls — that many people don’t follow me in my thinking and in how I assess things,” Merz said. “That’s my responsibility, and I accept it. I’ll try to do things differently — to do better — in the coming weeks and months.” The question is whether his party will be that patient.

https://www.dw.com/en/hundreds-of-french.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nkg4 The school protests have spread nationwide, as here in Lyon Image: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Several hundred schools in France closed totally or partially on Monday amid security fears following a wave of nationwide student protests, the education minister has said. The protests by pupils complaining of poor conditions began at one Paris school on September 17 but last week mutated into sometimes violent demonstrations across the nation. France students protest school conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Why are the schools staying closed? Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be totally or partly suspended in some 400 to 500 high schools on Monday, as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled." According to Geffray, the schools were being closed mainly as a precaution, with more large protests planned for Tuesday. Geffray said the number of schools remaining closed on Monday would be similar to that on Friday but that there was planned to be a "partial, progressive return to lessons." He said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff members injured since the protests began. "There are activists — particularly from the far left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Geffray said. "Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he added. Several schools have been damaged amid the protests Image: CLPRESS/ABACA/picture alliance Valerie Pecresse, the president of the Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital, said that more than a third of the 468 schools in the region would be shut on Monday. What are the school protesters saying? The protesting teenagers at French upper high schools, called lycees, have complained of high rates of absenteeism by teachers, school days that are too long and dilapidated facilities. They have also protested at the lack of adequate cooling on hot summer days, with some towns seeing temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) last summer in a country without widespread air conditioning. Organizers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government was still failing to propose "concrete measures" to remedy the situation. On Sunday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu urged local authorities to make it a priority to fill gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts. He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss renovating school buildings that are often in poor condition. Violent incidents at the school protests The protests have been marked by several violent incidents, with security forces sometimes using tear gas and batons to disperse the young protesters. More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement. On Sunday, a 16-year-old was detained after a 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a protest in the southern town of La Ciotat. Last week, a group of young people was filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in the eastern town of Belfort. The French branch of rights group Amnesty International last week described the action taken by police as "disproportionate." Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has, however, defended security forces, saying they were "not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands."
